content: 1. The use of tetracycline-class drugs, including doxycycline monohydrate, during tooth development (the last half of pregnancy, infancy, and childhood up to 8 years of age) can result in permanent discoloration of the teeth, ranging from yellow to gray to brown. This adverse effect is more common with prolonged use but has also been observed after repeated short-term courses. Enamel hypoplasia has also been reported. Therefore, tetracycline drugs should not be used in this age group unless treating anthrax (including inhalational anthrax post-exposure) when no other effective drugs are available or suitable. 2. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including doxycycline monohydrate capsules. The severity can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if it occurs up to two months after the last dose. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotics not targeting C. difficile may be necessary, along with appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy, and surgical evaluation as clinically indicated. 3. Tetracyclines form a stable calcium complex in bone-forming tissues. A decrease in fibula growth rate has been observed in premature infants given oral tetracycline at doses of 25 mg/kg every six hours. This effect was shown to be reversible upon discontinuation of the drug. Animal studies indicate that tetracyclines cross the placenta, accumulate in fetal tissues, and can exert toxic effects on the developing fetus, often related to skeletal development retardation. Evidence of embryotoxicity has been noted in animals treated early in pregnancy. If tetracyclines are used during pregnancy or if a patient becomes pregnant while taking these drugs, the patient should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. 4. The anti-anabolic action of tetracyclines may lead to an increase in blood urea nitrogen (BUN). However, studies indicate that this does not occur with doxycycline use in patients with impaired renal function. 5. Photosensitivity, characterized by an exaggerated sunburn reaction, has been observed in some individuals taking tetracyclines. Patients who are likely to be exposed to direct sunlight or ultraviolet light should be warned about this potential reaction, and treatment should be discontinued at the first sign of skin erythema. 6. As with other antibiotics, the use of doxycycline may result in the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, including fungi. If superinfection occurs, the antibiotic should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. 7. Bulging fontanels in infants and benign intracranial hypertension in adults have been reported in individuals receiving tetracyclines. These conditions resolved upon discontinuation of the drug. 8. Surgical procedures, such as incision and drainage, should be performed alongside antibiotic therapy when indicated. 9. Prescribing doxycycline monohydrate capsules in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 10. Patients should be advised to drink plenty of fluids while taking doxycycline to reduce the risk of esophageal irritation and ulceration. 11. The absorption of tetracyclines is reduced when taken with foods containing calcium. However, the absorption of doxycycline is not significantly affected by simultaneous ingestion of food or milk. 12. The absorption of tetracyclines is impaired by bismuth subsalicylate, antacids containing aluminum, calcium, or magnesium, and iron-containing preparations. 13. Barbiturates, carbamazepine, and phenytoin decrease the half-life of doxycycline. 14. Concurrent use of tetracyclines and methoxyflurane has been reported to result in fatal renal toxicity. 15. Tetracyclines may render oral contraceptives less effective. 16. False elevations of urinary catecholamine levels may occur due to interference with fluorescence tests. 17. Long-term studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of doxycycline have not been conducted. However, related antibiotics, such as oxytetracycline and minocycline, have shown evidence of oncogenic activity in animal studies. Mutagenicity studies of doxycycline have not been conducted, but related antibiotics have shown positive results in in vitro mammalian cell assays. 18. Doxycycline administered orally at high doses (up to 250 mg/kg/day) had no apparent effect on the fertility of female rats. The effect on male fertility has not been studied. 19. Doxycycline is classified as Pregnancy Category D. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies on the use of doxycycline in pregnant women. A weak but marginally statistically significant association with congenital malformations has been observed in case-control studies. Patients should be informed of the potential risks if doxycycline is used during pregnancy. 20. The effect of tetracyclines on labor and delivery is unknown. 21. Tetracyclines are excreted in human milk, but the extent of absorption by the breastfed infant is not known. Due to the potential for adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. 22. Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including doxycycline monohydrate capsules, should only be used to treat bacterial infections. They should be informed that skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may decrease the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 23. In cases of venereal disease where coexistent syphilis is suspected, a dark-field examination should be performed before treatment, and blood serology should be repeated monthly for at least four months. 24. During long-term therapy, periodic laboratory evaluations of organ systems, including hematopoietic, renal, and hepatic studies, should be conducted. 25. Tetracyclines have been shown to depress plasma prothrombin activity, so patients on anticoagulant therapy may require dosage adjustments. 26. Bacteriostatic drugs, such as tetracyclines, may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillin, so concurrent use should be avoided.
